content: A red giant is a highly luminous giant star that has a low to intermediate mass and is in the later stages of its stellar evolution. The core of a red giant is composed of electron-degenerate matter, which is extremely compressed. This compression causes the outer layers of the star to expand and become tenuous, resulting in an enormous radius and a relatively low surface temperature, typically below 5,000 Kelvin. The appearance of red giants ranges from yellow-orange to red, corresponding to spectral types K and M, as well as certain class S stars and most carbon stars. The most common type of red giants are Red Giant Branch (RGB) stars, which continue to fuse hydrogen in a shell surrounding an inert helium core. Another category of red giants, known as Asymptotic Giant Branch (AGB) stars, produce carbon through the triple-alpha process in their helium cores. AGB stars include carbon stars of types C-N and late C-R. Notable examples of bright red giants visible in the night sky include Arcturus (Alpha Bootis), Aldebaran (Alpha Tauri), Pollux (Beta Geminorum), and Gamma Crucis (Gacrux). Red giants are stars that have exhausted the hydrogen in their cores and now fuse hydrogen in a shell outside the core. These stars can have radii tens to hundreds of times larger than the Sun. The inert helium core contracts and heats up due to the lack of an energy source, compressing the hydrogen shell above it and accelerating hydrogen fusion. This process increases the star's luminosity by 1,000 to 10,000 times and causes the outer layers to expand. The expansion outpaces the increase in luminosity, leading to a decrease in the star's effective temperature. In stars massive enough to ignite helium fusion, a similar process occurs when the central helium is depleted, and helium fusion begins in a shell. In many cases, hydrogen fusion continues in a separate shell at a shallower depth, placing the star on the Asymptotic Giant Branch. The cooling of the star's surface shifts its visible light output toward the red spectrum, giving it the characteristic red giant appearance, though the color is often more orange than red. Main sequence stars of spectral types A through K are believed to evolve into red giants. Very low-mass stars, which are fully convective, may not develop an inert helium core and could burn through all their fuel without becoming red giants. These stars, known as red dwarfs, have lifespans much longer than the current age of the universe, so no observations of their aging exist. In contrast, very high-mass stars evolve into supergiants, which oscillate horizontally across the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram. At the right end of this diagram, they become red supergiants, which typically end their lives as Type II supernovae. For stars with masses around 0.5 to 2.5 solar masses, the addition of helium to the core from shell hydrogen fusion can trigger a helium flash—a rapid burst of helium fusion in the core. After this event, the star enters a brief phase of helium fusion before ascending the red giant branch again. Stars with masses between 2.5 and about 4 to 6 solar masses transition into the helium-fusing phase more smoothly. This phase, known as the horizontal branch in metal-poor stars, is so named because these stars form a nearly horizontal line in the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram of star clusters. Metal-rich helium-fusing stars, however, do not lie on the horizontal branch but instead form a clump, referred to as the red clump, in the diagram. Red giants are not sharply defined spheres with distinct edges, as often depicted in images. Due to their very low density, these stars may lack a well-defined photosphere and instead have a body that gradually transitions into a corona. In approximately 5 billion years, the Sun is expected to become a red giant. During this phase, it will expand sufficiently to engulf the current orbits of some inner planets, including Earth. However, the Sun will lose a significant portion of its mass during this transformation, causing the orbits of most planets, except Mercury and Venus, to widen. Earth's fate is uncertain. While it might escape engulfment by moving to a wider orbit, tidal interactions between the Sun and Earth could cause Earth to spiral inward, ultimately being engulfed and incorporated into the Sun before the Sun reaches its maximum size. This would occur despite the Sun losing about 38% of its mass. Before this engulfment, Earth's biosphere will have already been destroyed due to the Sun's gradual increase in brightness as its hydrogen supply diminishes and its core contracts. This destruction will occur well before the Sun transitions into a red giant. Over the next billion years, Earth's atmosphere and lithosphere will become similar to those of Venus. Eventually, most of Earth's atmosphere will be lost to space, leaving behind a desiccated, lifeless planet with a surface of molten rock.
